chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Said from Muhammad ibn Abi Umayr from Al-Hakam ibn 'Ubayya al-Asadi said:

I was appointed to Bahrain and acquired much wealth there, so I spent it and bought many estates, and I bought slaves and mothers of children, and children were born to me. Then I went to Mecca, taking my dependents, mothers of my children, and my wives, and I took one-fifth of that wealth. I entered upon Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) and said to him: 'I was appointed to Bahrain and acquired much wealth there, bought goods, slaves, mothers of children, and children were born to me, and I spent it. Here is the one-fifth of that wealth, and these are the mothers of my children and my wives; I have brought them to you.' He said: 'Indeed, all of it is for us, and I have accepted what you brought. I have made permissible for you the mothers of your children and your wives and what you spent, and I have guaranteed for you, upon me and upon my father, Paradise.'

key_terms.أُمَّهَاتِ أَوْلاَدٍ: Mothers of children (female slaves who bore children)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on khums of wealth acquired by a governor or official in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* illustrates the Shia doctrine of the Imam’s absolute ownership (*Milk al-Khass*) over the khums of the faithful, where the Imam accepts the one-fifth portion as a spiritual and legal transfer of rights. Imam al-Baqir’s declaration that 'all of it is for us' underscores the divine authority of the Imam in managing wealth, while his specific grant of the companion’s family and expenditures serves as a practical mechanism for purification (*Tathir*), ensuring the remaining four-fifths become halal. The guarantee of Paradise links the financial obligation to spiritual salvation, a key theme in Shia jurisprudence regarding the purifying nature of khums.
